subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Default Heuristic
description: A quick, practical guide to The Default Heuristic.

hook.text: Austria has 99% organ donation. Germany has 12%. The only difference: Austria's form opts you in by default.

buildup.text: Johnson and Goldstein showed that default options dominate. Most people never switch from what's pre-selected.

discovery.text: The default heuristic: when we're unsure or busy, we accept whatever is pre-chosen. Defaults are powerful.

twist.text: This isn't laziness. People interpret defaults as recommendations. 'They must have set it this way for a reason.'

climax.text: Whoever designs the default designs the outcome. Most people will never change it.

punchline.text: The default usually wins. Choose it wisely.

quiz.question: Why do people tend to stick with defaults?
options: They always agree with the designer's choice
They view defaults as recommendations and switching takes effort
Defaults are always the best option

details.summary: The default heuristic is the tendency to accept pre-set options without active deliberation. People treat defaults as implicit recommendations, and the effort required to change from the default creates a barrier that most people do not overcome regardless of their actual preferences.
details.whyItMatters: Default settings shape organ donation rates, retirement savings, privacy settings, and consumer choices for millions of people.
takeaways: Most people accept default options without considering alternatives
Defaults are perceived as implicit recommendations from the choice architect
Changing defaults is the most powerful nudge available to policy designers

faq.question: Why are defaults so powerful in shaping behavior?
faq.answer: Three forces converge: effort avoidance means changing requires action while accepting does not; implied recommendation means the default feels endorsed by whoever set it; and loss aversion means switching away from the default feels like giving up the guaranteed option.

faq.question: What is the most dramatic example of default power?
faq.answer: Organ donation rates in opt-in countries average around 15 percent while opt-out countries average over 90 percent. The medical preferences of the populations are similar; the difference is entirely driven by which option is the default.
